newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary says crime hurts image, more police needed.
newsitem.headline: Hungary says crime hurts image, more police needed.

text.p: Hungarian Interior Minister Gabor Kuncze said on Friday that Hungary will field thousands more police to fight rising crime and clamp down on tourist rip-offs that tarnished Hungary's image abroad.

"Our objective is to take very resolute action," Kuncze said at a news conference announcing plans to add 4,000 to Hungary's 40,000-man police force and seek government approval for a $200 million police spending package over three years.
Hungary has suffered a spate of bombings police say were linked to a tax-evasion scheme and reports in the Hungarian media on extortionate rip-offs of tourists.
One report told of an American packpacker being forced to pay more than $1,000 on his credit card for a few drinks he had with two women at a cafe in the main tourist area of Budapest.

The U.S. Embassy in Budapest this week sent a notice to English-language newspapers in Hungary advising Americans to stay out of five restaurants and clubs in Budapest where it said there had been "excessive billing of customers" or physical intimidation or assault of patrons.

Kuncze said reports in the foreign press may have exaggerated the extent of Hungary's problem. But he acknowledged statistics showed crime had soared almost 110 percent from 1990-1995 from well below average for Europe in the last years of communism to about average.
"This is the explanation why people's sense of security has declined so much," Kuncze said.
"It is the dynamic that the Hungarian public sees as being so bad, although even with this Hungary has only arrived in the middle of the field."
Kuncze said scams such as restaurants failing to disclose full prices or people posing as "tourist police" to extort money from visitors were bad for Hungary's image.
"Our objective is to take very resolute action...because it puts Hungary in a bad light and causes more damage to the reputation of the country than some routine crime," he said.
Chief Police Commissioner Laszlo Forgacs said police recently arrested some Romanians who had posed as tourist police to bilk tourists of thousands of dollars.
But he added that Hungarian law sometimes posed an obstacle to police clamping down on illegal activity, such as drug sales in discotheques.
"The public administration has no instrument to close down these discotheques," he said.
The plan to increase the police budget will be discussed by the government next week and would have to be submitted to Parliament for approval, police officials said.
